title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The preregistered primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task reused across arms); guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic network verifier. All paired episodes were scored safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics produced identical shared candidates that passed deterministic validation in every task, no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and the paired contrast is degenerate. We report the preregistered design, execution accounting, artifact‑grounded analysis, and a failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome, and provide concrete artifact‑grounded recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Translating high‑level operator intent to device configuration safely and reliably is a central operational goal. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows promise rapid intent→configuration translation, but text‑level metrics miss ordering, dependency, and invariants required for safe application to live devices. Execution‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are applied to emulated devices and deterministically scored—exposes semantic failures (ordering mistakes, transient violations, protected‑resource touches) that text‑only tests often miss [1].

A widely proposed architectural pattern to mitigate such failures is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM generates a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations are detected [2], [3]. Prior work demonstrates GVR‑style approaches can reduce syntactic and many semantic faults in benchmarked settings, but open questions remain about empirical verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompts, and about paired experimental designs that can detect causal verifier effects [2], [4], [5].

We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment to measure the paired difference in unsafe_apply rate between an LLM‑only baseline and a GVR guarded pipeline. The execution adhered to shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across both arms). This manuscript (1) describes the preregistered estimand and paired design; (2) maps the archived, artifact‑grounded analysis onto the estimand; and (3) explains why the paired contrast was degenerate in this run and how future experiments can produce informative contrasts.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks for LLM NetOps agents have recently been proposed to move evaluation from textual fidelity to execution correctness; NetConfArena exemplifies this trend [1]. Research on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and demonstrates that validators often enable high repair coverage for benchmarked faults, though semantic coverage depends on verifier design and the fault taxonomy [2], [4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising patterns for operational NetOps automation and safety [3], [5]. Engineering precedents (e.g., the evolution of Batfish) illustrate incremental verifier design and the importance of workload‑centred checks for reachability and invariants [6].

Our study differs by combining a preregistered paired estimand, shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, deterministic execution scoring, and full archival of per‑call traces and validator records to enable exact reconciliation between reported numbers and stored artifacts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the study (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline). A binary outcome per task (unsafe_apply = 1 vs safe_apply = 0) is determined by deterministic emulation and invariant checks after the arm's final output (for guarded arm: after up to one repair).

Design and generation semantics: The design is paired with shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single initial LLM generation was produced per task and reused for both the baseline and guarded episodes. Under this adapter contract, a paired difference can only arise if that shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation and the guarded pipeline applies a repair that changes the final configuration, or if the verifier and emulator disagree and exclusion rules or sensitivity treatments alter the analysis outcome. This semantic is a preregistered design choice intended to constrain model‑call budgets and to create a strict within‑task pairing.

Tasks, sampling, and adversary protocol: We executed N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks blocked into topology/vendor clusters. Task composition was: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48 tasks; novel topologies/vendors), and adversarial‑prompt 20% (48 tasks; adversarial prompts generated under the preregistered attacker seed). Tasks were deterministically generated and include input initial state, required command sequence, and workflow constraints.

Models, verifier, and adapter contract: The declared model used for generation was gpt-5-mini. The guarded pipeline integrated a deterministic network verifier that performs semantic invariant checks (ordering, group constraints, protected interfaces). The guarded arm was permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Runtime model sampling metadata were recorded for every model call; the shared_initial_candidate contract resulted in one initial generation per task.

Scoring, exclusions, and analysis executor: The primary analysis used a paired binary analysis: a paired contingency table, paired bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant pairs. Predeclared exclusions: pairs flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (verifier PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) would be excluded from the primary analysis and handled in sensitivity analyses; infra failures after the allowed retries would be excluded per the preregistration. The retry policy allowed up to two infra recovery attempts.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed according to the preregistered plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete pairs = 240. Exactly one shared initial generation was produced per task (model call budget adhered to the shared_initial_candidate contract). No infra failures, no unscorable episodes, and no preregistered exclusions occurred in this run.

Primary outcomes and contingency: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. The observed contingency counts were: n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 (guarded safe, baseline unsafe) = 0; n01 (guarded unsafe, baseline safe) = 0; n00 (both unsafe) = 0. Consequently, the paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. The bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.00, 0.00]. The exact McNemar two‑sided p‑value on discordant pairs is 1.0.

Validator activity and repair utilization: Across all guarded episodes the verifier passed every shared candidate and no validator‑triggered repairs were applied; therefore the guarded pipeline did not alter any final configuration relative to the shared initial candidate. Subgroup slices (in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, adversarial) are identical and exhibit zero unsafe applies in both arms.

Planned sensitivity channels unused: The preregistration included sensitivity analyses that would treat flagged 'possible false‑safe' items or infra failures as unsafe in worst‑case tests; because no such flags or failures occurred, these sensitivity channels were not engaged and yield no additional insight for this run.
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic explanation for the null paired contrast: The experimental semantics (shared_initial_candidate) produced a single generation per task that served both arms. In this run, every shared initial generation passed deterministic validation; because the guarded arm could only request up to one repair and none were invoked, the guarded arm could not create discordant pairs. Thus the null paired result is a direct consequence of the combination of generation semantics and verifier outcomes, not evidence that verifiers are unhelpful in general.

Design implications for informative GVR tests: To measure verifier effectiveness as a causal intervention, an experimental design must create opportunities for discordant outcomes. Three pragmatic options are: (A) allow independent initial generations per arm (so generator variability can produce candidates that selectively fail validation); (B) expand the repair budget and/or repair search strategy so the guarded pipeline can exercise repair behavior when validation fails; (C) strengthen adversarial protocols (e.g., adaptive adversaries or a broader adversary seed schedule) to increase initial candidate failure rates. Each option increases the probability that validator logic will be exercised and that repairs will change final outputs, producing non‑degenerate paired contrasts.

Threats to validity and artifact‑grounded caveats: Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate contract was an explicit design choice and limits causal interpretations to validator‑triggered repairs of a shared sample; this contract and its runtime adherence were enforced during execution. Construct validity: the deterministic verifier implements a finite check set; passing the verifier does not guarantee absence of every semantic class of failure. External validity: tasks were drawn from a synthetic emulation corpus and may not capture all production idiosyncrasies across vendors and operator workflows. Conclusion validity: the realized baseline unsafe rate was zero, which precludes detecting verifier benefit under the tested contract; power calculations in the preregistration assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate and different sampling dynamics.
sections.conclusion:
We executed a preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Observed outcome: all N = 240 paired episodes were safe under both arms, producing a paired difference of 0.00 (95% CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). This degenerate result is artifact‑grounded: the single shared initial generation per task passed deterministic validation in every case, so no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and thus no paired discordant outcomes could arise. Our artifact archive and analysis parameters (contingency counts, bootstrap resamples and seed, task composition, model call accounting) support this interpretation and motivate concrete experimental redesigns—independent generation per arm, wider repair budgets, or stronger adversary protocols—to create informative paired contrasts in future GVR evaluations. These recommendations are intended to help future work empirically quantify verifier benefit under operationally realistic perturbations and adversarial stressors.

disclosure_statement: Execution used declared model "gpt-5-mini" via the hosted adapter family. The guarded pipeline incorporated a deterministic network verifier identified in the execution record and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. Human role prior to the lock: the Research Director selected the NetOps topic family and constrained the initial master prompt. All literature search, experiment design, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. The preregistered generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract the paired contrast could only differ if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The execution manifest, per‑call traces, validator traces, task manifest, and analysis artifacts are archived and available for reproducibility inspection; no manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: the experiment used a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other models, prompting strategies, or prompt templates.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design produced one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes observed verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: the deterministic verifier implements a finite set of semantic checks; passing the verifier does not guarantee the absence of every potential semantic fault class.
